content: The study by Al-Makoshi (2013) analyzed breastfeeding data by categorizing it into Full Breastfeeding (defined as the age at which formula or other fluids, excluding water, were introduced) and Breastfeeding (defined as the age at which breastfeeding was stopped). For calculations, breastfeeding duration was used, with No Breastfeeding serving as the reference group. Odds ratios (ORs) were calculated for breastfeeding durations of greater than 12 months compared to 6–12 months. However, age-specific participant numbers were not provided. In Alho (1990), data on acute otitis media, otitis media with effusion, and respiratory tract infections were presented as adjusted ORs for breastfeeding durations of less than 3 months versus 7–11 months and greater than 12 months. Breastfeeding for less than 3 months was used as the reference group, and OR values were inverted for analysis. No data on single episodes of otitis media were provided; instead, otitis media proneness was defined as three or more episodes. Stuebe (2009) provided data on diabetes from two separate NHS cohorts. Hazard ratios (HRs) for breastfeeding durations of 6–11 months and 12–23 months were combined using the generic inverse variance (GIV) method, with No Breastfeeding as the reference group. Imputed HRs were calculated for breastfeeding durations of 12–23 months versus 7–12 months. For hypertension, breastfeeding for more than 12 months was the reference group, and comparisons were made with breastfeeding durations of 9 to less than 12 months. HRs were reversed for analysis. Peters (2017) compared cumulative breastfeeding durations, using 0–12 months as the comparison group. ORs for continued breastfeeding versus other durations were imputed. Lee (2005) analyzed cumulative breastfeeding durations, providing relative risks (RRs) for 13–18 months and 19–24 months of breastfeeding. These were analyzed separately and combined using the GIV method to compare with breastfeeding durations of 7–12 months. RRs for continued versus shorter breastfeeding durations were calculated, with No Breastfeeding as the reference group. Gay (2015) and Kim (2015) also provided RRs for continued and shorter breastfeeding durations, using No Breastfeeding as the reference group. RRs for continued versus shorter breastfeeding durations were calculated. Lupton (2013) presented data with 99% confidence intervals (CIs), which were converted to standard errors (SEs). Pooled data for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months were combined using the GIV method to calculate ORs for 12–24 months, with No Breastfeeding as the reference group. Natland (2012) converted geometric means of HDL, LDL, triglycerides, cholesterol, and blood glucose to arithmetic means. Age-stratified data were combined using the GIV method, with breastfeeding for more than 24 months as the reference group. ORs were imputed from this data. Cohen (2009) used No Breastfeeding as the reference group for ORs related to obesity. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus breastfeeding for 7–12 months. Zhang (2015) and Zhu (2020) provided ORs and adjusted mean differences, respectively, for various breastfeeding durations, using No Breastfeeding or breastfeeding for less than 3 months as the reference group. Imputed values were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus shorter durations. Daniels (2005) provided adjusted mean differences for normal and low birth weight children separately, without specifying the number of subjects in each group. SEs were calculated from upper and lower CIs, with breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group. Mean differences for continued breastfeeding (12–18 and 18–24 months) were imputed and pooled using a fixed-effect model. Song (2020) compared the risk of overweight/obesity in the 6–11 month breastfeeding group with those breastfeeding for more than 12 months, using the latter as the reference group. ORs were reversed for analysis. Li (2020) and Kim (2020a) provided ORs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and greater than 18 months, combining them using the GIV method. The reference groups were breastfeeding for 12 months and 3–6 months, respectively. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus 6 to less than 12 months. Jeon (2020) and Tan (2015) used HRs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and greater than 18 months, combining them using the GIV method. The reference groups were No Breastfeeding and breastfeeding for 12 months, respectively. Imputed HRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus 6 to less than 12 months. Gunderson (2018) used No Breastfeeding as the reference group and imputed HRs for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 6 to less than 12 months. Tanaka (2013) and Iida (2007) provided ORs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and greater than 18 months, combining them using the GIV method. The reference groups were breastfeeding for 0–6 months and 0 months, respectively. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus 6 to less than 12 months. Tanaka (2012) used prevalence ratios (PRs) for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and greater than 18 months, combining them using the GIV method. The reference group was breastfeeding for less than 6 months. Imputed PRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus 6 to less than 12 months. Olatosi (2014) compared the risk of early childhood caries (ECC) in the 7–12 month breastfeeding group with those breastfeeding for more than 12 months, using the latter as the reference group. ORs were reversed for analysis. Folayan (2010a) combined mean dmft index values for breastfeeding durations of 13–18 months and greater than 18 months for analysis. Christensen (2020) provided incidence rate ratios (IRRs) for hospitalization due to infection for breastfeeding durations of 7–9 months and 10–12 months. The IRR for the control group (7–12 months) was calculated by combining the two durations using the GIV method. The reference group was breastfeeding for 0–3 months. Imputed IRRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 13 months) versus 7–12 months. Fagerhaug (2013) provided SEs for breastfeeding durations of 7–12 months but not for the 13–24 month group. A web-plot application was used to manually extract means and CIs. The reference group was breastfeeding for more than 24 months. Imputed HRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (13–24 months) versus 7–12 months. Derakhshan (2017) calculated standard deviations (SDs) from 95% CIs. Values for breastfeeding durations of 13–18 months and 18–24 months were combined to calculate values for continued breastfeeding. Ki (2017) provided data for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months separately, which were combined for analysis. SEs were converted to SDs. The reference group was breastfeeding for 0–6 months. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding versus 7–12 months. Yeo (2016) provided data for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months, as well as for preand postmenopausal women, which were combined for analysis. Walby (2016) used Never Breastfed as the reference group. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 9–12 months. Nambiar (2013) provided data on male and female subjects separately, which were combined using the GIV method. The reference group was Never Breastfed. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 7–12 months. Abarca (2019) used Never Breastfed as the reference group. Imputed RRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 6–12 months. Pudla (2015) provided data for 7–10 years and 11–14 years separately. The odds ratio (OR) for obesity was combined using the GIV method. The reference group was Never Breastfed or Breastfed for less than 1 month. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 6–12 months. Liese (2001) used breastfeeding for less than 6 months as the reference group. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 6–12 months. De Siqueira (2007) compared the risk of obesity in the 6–11 month breastfeeding group with those breastfeeding for more than 12 months, using the latter as the reference group. ORs were reversed for analysis. Von Kries (1999) used No Breastfeeding as the reference group. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 6–12 months. Haag (2019) used No Breastfeeding as the reference group. Imputed PRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–24 months) versus less than 12 months. Villamor (2000) used breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group. Imputed PRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–18 months and greater than or equal to 19 months) versus 7–12 months. PRs for 12–18 months and greater than or equal to 19 months were combined using the GIV method. Victora (2006) provided adjusted means and 95% CIs for lipid profiles. SDs were derived from 95% CIs. The OR for obesity used continued breastfeeding as the reference group. For analysis, ORs were reversed. For anthropometry and body composition, means and SEs were provided, and SDs were derived from SEs. Victora (1984) approximated numbers from percentage figures provided in the published paper. Veena (2010) provided data for breastfeeding durations of 18–24 months and 12–18 months separately. Means and SDs were combined for analysis. Verbal fluency scores were given separately for animals and first names. Trygvadottir (2001) used breastfeeding for 0–6 weeks as the reference group. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–24 months) versus 7–12 months. Tehrani (2014) used breastfeeding for more than 24 months as the reference group. Imputed RRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–24 months) versus 7–12 months. Stuebe (2010) derived SDs from 95% CIs. Stendel-Hollis (2013) combined HRs for four groups of continued breastfeeding and the control group using the GIV method. The reference group was No Breastfeeding. Imputed HRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–24 months) versus 4–12 months. Stuebe (2009a) combined HRs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 19+ months using the GIV method. The reference group was No Breastfeeding. Imputed HRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–24 months) versus the control group. Sichieri (2003) provided data for women with BMI less than and greater than 25, as well as for nulliparous and primiparous women, separately. Means and SDs for the four groups were combined for analysis. Adjusted mean difference SDs were unavailable, so unadjusted values were used. Oddy (2010) provided the percentage of children breastfed for varying durations at the beginning of the study and the total number of subjects at the end. It was assumed that the percentage remained constant, and the number of subjects was derived from these figures. Owen (2002) provided cholesterol and LDL values in mmol/L. Novaes (2012) compared the risk of obesity in the 6–11 month breastfeeding group with those breastfeeding for more than 12 months, using the latter as the reference group. ORs were reversed for analysis. Retnakumari (2012) derived data from Figure 3 using the Automeris app. Rajaei (2016) and Harvey (2009) derived data using the Automeris web-plot digitizer app. Muniz (2015) provided data for men and women separately, which were combined. SDs were derived from 95% CIs. Martin (2002) and Lima (2019) derived data using the Automeris web-plot digitizer app. Lima (2019) provided adjusted mean differences with breastfeeding for greater than or equal to 12 months as the reference group. Values were reversed for quantitative analysis, and biochemistry values were converted to mmol/L for analysis. Izadi (2013) used Never Breastfed as the reference group. Imputed ORs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (greater than 12 months) versus 7–12 months. ORs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months were provided separately and combined using the GIV method. Horta (2006) derived SDs from 95% CIs. Means and CIs for males and females were provided separately and combined. Hartwig (2019) used breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group. Imputed RRs were calculated for continued breastfeeding (12–23 months) versus 6–11 months. Duazo (2010) provided data for 5and 6-year-olds separately, with the total number of subjects for the two groups combined. It was assumed that the number of subjects for each age group was proportional to the total number given. Camurdan (2011) provided BMI means and SDs separately for appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) and large-for-gestational-age (LGA) babies, which were combined for quantitative analysis. Stordal (2017) provided adjusted RRs with breastfeeding for greater than or equal to 12 months as the reference group. Values were reversed for quantitative analysis. RRs for upper and lower respiratory infections were combined using the GIV method to calculate RRs for all respiratory tract infections. Nirunsittirat (2016) used breastfeeding for 0–6 months as the reference group. RRs for continued breastfeeding versus 6–11 months were calculated. RRs for breastfeeding durations of 12–18 months and greater than or equal to 18 months were provided separately.
